finding.claim: GET /invoice/<inv_id> returns any invoice by ID with no authentication or ownership check (IDOR / broken object-level authorization). The sibling route /my/invoice/<inv_id> enforces inv["customer"] == g.user["id"], so the missing check on this route looks like an oversight.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled URL path parameter inv_id on a public Flask route. No login is required, and the attacker only needs to guess or enumerate invoice IDs.
finding.sink: jsonify(inv) at invoices.py:10 returns the full invoice record, including the customer field and any other data in INVOICES, for any customer.

trace.note: @app.route("/invoice/<inv_id>") registers the route with no auth decorator.
INVOICES.get(inv_id) looks up the record by the attacker-supplied key and aborts with 404 only if it is missing.
The record is returned to the caller without comparing inv["customer"] to g.user. Compare the protected variant at invoices.py:16-17.

finding.guards_checked: The file has no before_request hook, login_required decorator, or middleware. The only ownership check is at lines 16-17, in the other route. I could not check whether an unseen layer such as a WSGI middleware or reverse proxy adds authentication, because only invoices.py exists in the repo. Even with authentication added, this route would still allow cross-tenant reads. Repro: curl http://host/invoice/<other_customers_id> returns 200 with the invoice JSON. The same ID on /my/invoice/<id> returns 404 for a non-owner.

verdict.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers /invoice/<inv_id> with no auth decorator or hook and returns jsonify(inv) without the ownership check that invoices.py:16-17 applies in the sibling route; no middleware exists in the repo (only invoices.py), though an external proxy can't be ruled out.
